About us

A cooperative the valley owns

Sham Valley Apricot Producer Cooperative Limited brings together 563 farmer members in 14 producer groups across 14 villages of lower Sham valley, Leh.

The place

One harvest a year, at the top of the country

Ladakh became a Union Territory on 31 October 2019. Its two districts, Leh and Kargil, are home to 2.74 lakh people, and four in five belong to Scheduled Tribes.

Terrain
Cold desert, about 4,000 m above sea level
Settlement
Low population density, scattered hamlets
Season
One cropping season per year
Crops
Niche crops, apricot chief among them
Status
Union Territory since 31 Oct 2019

Why a value chain

Plenty of fruit, too little reaching market

The valleys grow apricots in volume, yet farmers had no surplus to sell in an organised way. The idea was incubated with several funding agencies and grew into a centre for apricot in the lower Indus.

15,789 MT a year

of apricots grown across 45 villages, but held back by

  • Lack of marketable surplus produce
  • No package of practices (PoPs) for cultivation
  • Unorganised marketing

Centre for apricot

Sham Valley, lower Indus

  • Apricot FPO owned by its growers
  • Drying and packaging
  • Branding and marketing
STEP 1

Thematic, value-chain approach

Start from one commodity that matters to tribal livelihoods in the cold desert.

STEP 2

The product becomes the FPO's foundation

The identified product, apricot, became the basis for establishing the producer organisation.

STEP 3

Read demand, standardise supply

Assess market demand and standardise the product through strengthened backward linkages.

Why an FPO?

Sparse population, low productivity, heavy wastage and high operating costs, for a key commodity in the livelihoods of tribal families in Ladakh's cold desert.

The cooperative

A producer company the valley owns

Registered under the J&K Self-Reliant Cooperatives Act of 1999, the FPO operates its own processing unit and sells under its brand.

What still holds growth back

Four open challenges

Technical guidance

No centre of excellence for apricot, PoPs, input supply or post-harvest technology yet.

Limited data

Little reliable data on production, varieties and markets.

GI tag for Halman

Geographical Indication for the Halman apricot varieties is still pending.

Logistics

Moving perishable fruit out of a remote, high-altitude region.

Future strategy

A time-bound path to a self-reliant FPO

The FPO life cycle moves through four stages. At each one, dependency on Himmotthan Society (HMS) falls and the FPO takes on more of the work.

0–3 YEARS

Incubation

Formation, registration and pilot business

HMS dependency80–90%
Intensive handholding
Focus
Institution building and proof of concept
Key outputs
Basic compliance, initial turnover, member mobilisation
3–5 YEARS

Stabilisation

Co-management and systems building

HMS dependency50–60%
Shared responsibility
Focus
Governance, finance, MIS and HR systems
Key outputs
Functional board and CEO, regular accounts, stable operations
5–10 YEARS

Transition and expansion

FPO-led operations with an operational self-sufficiency focus

HMS dependency20–30%
Mentoring support
Focus
Business expansion and diversification
Key outputs
Break-even or profit, strong market and finance linkages
10+ YEARS

Sustainability

Full ownership and accountability with the FPO

HMS dependency<10%
On-call advisory only
Focus
Scaling, federation and ecosystem leadership
Key outputs
100% operational self-sufficiency, consistent surplus, peer mentoring role

Home/Value chain

Our value chain

From orchard to pouch

Members harvest and dry. Producer groups collect and do a first sort. The FPO grades, packs, brands and markets.

Farm to you

The journey of a Sham Valley apricot

Five stages, from orchards at around 4,000 m in Ladakh's cold desert to your door.

  1. 1
    Stage 1 · Orchard

    Orchards in the cold desert

    Apricot is a key crop for tribal families in Ladakh, where there is one cropping season a year. Across 45 villages, orchards produce about 15,789 MT of apricots annually. Member farmers are trained on the apricot package of practices and receive inputs such as bio-foliar fertiliser and bio-pesticides.

    • About 4,000 m above sea level
    • 14 villages of lower Sham valley
    • One cropping season a year
  2. 2
    Stage 2 · Harvesting

    Harvested by member families

    When the fruit ripens, member families harvest it with harvesting nets provided through the programme. Fruit for fresh sale is packed in the orchard, and the rest is dried by the families using apricot solar dryers.

    • 563 member farmers
    • 245 women members
    • Harvesting nets and solar dryers
  3. 3
    Stage 3 · Processing

    Collected, sorted and graded

    Producer groups collect the produce from members and do a first-level sort. At the FPO's processing unit, dried apricots are sorted, graded and standardised, and apricot stones are decorticated so the kernels can be pressed for oil.

    • 14 producer groups
    • First-level sorting at group level
    • Kernel oil extraction
  4. 4
    Stage 4 · Packaging

    Packed under the Julley Ladakh brand

    Dried apricots are packed in 250 g and 500 g pouches and apricot oil is bottled, then labelled and priced at the FPO unit. Fresh apricots go to a solar pre-cooling unit before dispatch.

    • Packaging, labelling and pricing
    • Solar pre-cooling for fresh fruit
  5. 5
    Stage 5 · From FPO to customer

    From the cooperative to you

    The FPO markets the range itself, linking Sham valley to domestic, institutional and export buyers. Fresh apricots are air-freighted in season, and in 2023 the cooperative won the CII Excellence Award for Best FPO Market Linkage.
